plan: Nine new items applying batch 14's feedback: vocabulary choices are all uncommon words so elimination by familiarity fails; a computed-count data item; S014-03 resubmitted relabelled easy. S014-05 is not resubmitted (disputed usage).

passages.title: Seven volumes
passages.text: Reviewers called the biographer's account ______: across seven volumes it records nearly every letter the composer wrote, every rehearsal she attended, and every illness she suffered.

passages.title: Regrowing limbs
passages.text: Early naturalists regarded the axolotl's ability to regrow lost limbs as an ______, a strange exception among animals with backbones, but biologists now know that several other salamanders share the ability.

passages.title: Seedling density
passages.text:
Researchers planted tree seedlings at four densities and recorded the percentage still alive after one year.
Seedlings planted per square meter | 10 | 20 | 40 | 80
Percentage surviving | 90% | 75% | 55% | 40%
A student claims that even though the survival rate fell as density increased, the number of surviving seedlings per square meter rose.

passages.title: Bright plumage
passages.text: In many bird species, males with brighter plumage attract more mates, but bright colors also make males easier for predators to spot. If predation is what keeps male plumage from becoming even brighter, then researchers studying a population of one such species on an island with no bird predators would expect males there to ______

passages.title: Restoring the mills
passages.text: Restoring the town's three abandoned textile mills, along with the network of canals that once powered their looms, ______ more than a decade and cost nearly twice the original estimate.

passages.title: The Rosetta Stone
passages.text: The Rosetta Stone ______ in 1799 by French soldiers near the Egyptian town of Rashid, carries the same decree in three scripts, a feature that later helped scholars decipher Egyptian hieroglyphs.

passages.title: Bamboo
passages.text: Bamboo grows remarkably quickly, with some species reaching their full height in a single growing season. ______ it can be harvested without killing the plant, which sends up new shoots from its underground roots.

passages.title: Muralist notes
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Elena Varga (1921–1987) was a Hungarian-born muralist who worked in Chicago.
• Her best-known work, Harvest Line, covers a 200-foot wall of a former rail depot.
• The mural shows grain workers loading freight cars.
• Varga painted it in 1958 using donated house paint.

passages.title: Rising bedrock
passages.text: For decades, geologists assumed that the bedrock beneath large ice sheets rose only very slowly after the ice above it thinned. Recent measurements beneath part of the West Antarctic Ice Sheet, however, show the ground there rising by several centimeters a year as the ice thins, because the underlying rock flows unusually easily. Some researchers suggest that this rapid rise could eventually help slow the ice sheet's retreat by lifting the base of the ice.

passages.title: Teaching methods
passages.text:
A district compared average test scores of students taught with two reading methods at urban and rural schools.
School type | Method A | Method B
Urban | 72 | 75
Rural | 64 | 73
A researcher claims that Method B's advantage over Method A was greater at rural schools than at urban schools.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
candidates.evidence: it records nearly every letter the composer wrote
candidates.explanation: An account that covers nearly every letter, rehearsal and illness is thorough to the point of completeness: "exhaustive."

A.rationale: "Laconic" means using very few words, the opposite of a seven-volume account.

C.rationale: A perfunctory account would be hasty and superficial, not one that records nearly everything.

D.rationale: "Tendentious" means biased toward a point of view; nothing in the text describes bias.

hints: What does the colon clause tell you about the account?
candidates.remember: Predict a word from the clause after the colon before reading the choices.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
candidates.evidence: a strange exception among animals with backbones
candidates.explanation: The appositive defines the blank: "a strange exception" is an anomaly.

B.rationale: An archetype is a typical model, the opposite of "a strange exception."

C.rationale: An imposition is an unwelcome burden; nothing suggests the ability was a burden.

D.rationale: An embellishment is a decorative addition, not an exception to a pattern.

hints: What phrase right after the blank defines it?

strategy.explanation: Use the appositive as the definition.

candidates.remember: An appositive after a blank often defines it.

candidates.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the student's claim?

choices.A: The survival rate fell steadily from 90% at the lowest density to only 40% at the highest density of 80 per square meter.
choices.B: At a density of 20 seedlings per square meter, 75% of the seedlings planted were still alive after one full year of growth.
choices.C: At 80 per square meter, about 32 seedlings per square meter survived, compared with about 9 at 10 per square meter.
choices.D: At 40 seedlings per square meter, 55% survived, a higher survival rate than the 40% seen at 80 seedlings per square meter.

candidates.evidence: the number of surviving seedlings per square meter rose
candidates.explanation: Survivors per square meter = density × survival rate: 10 × 0.90 = 9 and 80 × 0.40 = 32. Only C states the numbers of survivors, which rose.

A.rationale: This shows survival rates falling, the part of the claim that is conceded, not the rise in survivors.

B.rationale: A single density cannot show that the number of survivors rose as density increased.

D.rationale: This compares survival rates, not the number of surviving seedlings.

hints: The claim is about the number of survivors, not the percentage. How do you get a number from a percentage?

strategy.explanation: Multiply each density by its survival rate.

candidates.remember: Distinguish a rate from a count: multiply to get the count.

candidates.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: attract fewer mates on average than males of the same species living on the mainland.
choices.B: be duller on average, because producing bright feathers is costly in any environment.
choices.C: show no difference in brightness from males of the same species on the mainland.
choices.D: be brighter on average than males of the same species living on the predator-rich mainland.

candidates.evidence: If predation is what keeps male plumage from becoming even brighter
candidates.explanation: If predators are the limit, then where there are no predators the limit is lifted, so island males should be brighter.

A.rationale: Nothing about the hypothesis suggests island males would attract fewer mates.

B.rationale: The hypothesis concerns predation; this introduces a different explanation.

C.rationale: If predation limits brightness, removing predators should change brightness.

hints: What happens to a limit when its cause is removed?

strategy.explanation: Remove predators and follow the hypothesis.

candidates.remember: "If X limits Y" predicts more Y where X is absent.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: Restoring the town's three abandoned textile mills
candidates.explanation: The subject is the activity "Restoring the town's three abandoned textile mills," a singular gerund phrase. "Along with ..." does not make it plural, and "cost" shows the past tense: "took."

A.rationale: The subject is the gerund phrase "Restoring ...," which is singular; "have" is plural.

B.rationale: "Were" is plural and does not agree with the singular gerund subject.

C.rationale: "Taking" leaves the sentence without a main verb.

hints: Is the subject the mills or the act of restoring them?

strategy.explanation: Find the true subject; ignore "along with."

candidates.remember: A gerund-phrase subject is singular, whatever nouns follow it.

candidates.subskill: Commas around a nonessential participial phrase
candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: near the Egyptian town of Rashid, carries
candidates.explanation: "Rediscovered in 1799 ... Rashid" is extra information about the stone, so it is set off by a pair of commas; the second comma is already in place before "carries."

A.rationale: Without a comma before it, the phrase is not set off, yet a comma follows it before "carries."

C.rationale: "Which rediscovered" makes the stone the one doing the rediscovering.

D.rationale: A semicolon would separate the subject "The Rosetta Stone" from its verb "carries."

hints: Is there already a comma at the end of the phrase?

strategy.explanation: Match the comma that closes the phrase.

candidates.remember: Nonessential phrases need commas on both sides.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
candidates.evidence: it can be harvested without killing the plant
candidates.explanation: The second sentence adds a further, separate advantage of bamboo: "Moreover."

A.rationale: Being harvestable without dying is another advantage, not a contrast with fast growth.

B.rationale: Regrowing after harvest is not an example of growing quickly.

D.rationale: Growing quickly does not cause the plant to survive harvest.

hints: Is the second sentence a contrast, an example, a result, or an additional point?
candidates.remember: Addition transitions join two separate points in the same direction.

candidates.subskill: Rhetorical synthesis (introducing an artist and work)
candidates.stem: The student wants to introduce Harvest Line to an audience unfamiliar with Elena Varga. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Harvest Line, which shows grain workers loading freight cars, was painted in 1958 with donated house paint.
choices.B: Elena Varga, who lived from 1921 to 1987, was a Hungarian-born muralist who did most of her work in Chicago.
choices.C: The 200-foot mural Harvest Line, Elena Varga's best-known work, covers a wall of a former rail depot.
choices.D: Hungarian-born Chicago muralist Elena Varga painted Harvest Line, a 200-foot scene of grain workers, in 1958.

candidates.evidence: Elena Varga (1921–1987) was a Hungarian-born muralist who worked in Chicago.
candidates.explanation: An unfamiliar audience needs to know who Varga was and what the mural is. Only A gives both: her background and the work.

A.rationale: This describes the mural but does not introduce Varga to readers who do not know her.

B.rationale: This introduces Varga but not Harvest Line.

C.rationale: This names Varga but does not tell an unfamiliar audience who she was.

hints: What does an audience unfamiliar with the artist need to learn?

strategy.explanation: Note both parts of the goal.

candidates.remember: Introducing to a new audience: identify the person and the work.

candidates.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Geologists have long known that bedrock beneath ice sheets rises rapidly whenever the ice above it thins.
choices.B: The West Antarctic Ice Sheet is thinning more quickly than any other ice sheet that researchers have measured.
choices.C: Bedrock under some Antarctic ice is rising faster than once assumed, which might help slow the ice's retreat.
choices.D: Rising bedrock beneath Antarctica will soon stop the retreat of the West Antarctic Ice Sheet entirely.

candidates.evidence: show the ground there rising by several centimeters a year as the ice thins
candidates.explanation: The text contrasts the old assumption (slow rise) with new measurements (rapid rise) and ends with a possible consequence (slowing retreat). C captures all of this without overstating it.

A.rationale: The text says geologists long assumed the rise was slow.

B.rationale: The text does not compare thinning rates among ice sheets.

D.rationale: Researchers say it "could" help slow the retreat, not that it will stop it.

hints: What do the new measurements overturn, and what might follow?

strategy.explanation: Eliminate choices that contradict or overstate.

candidates.remember: Main ideas avoid both distortion and overstatement.

candidates.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the researcher's claim?

choices.A: At rural schools Method B students outscored Method A students by 9 points, compared with 3 points at urban schools.
choices.B: Students taught with Method B scored higher at urban schools, averaging 75, than at rural schools, averaging 73.
choices.C: At both urban and rural schools, students taught with Method B outscored students taught with Method A on average.
choices.D: Rural students taught with Method A had the lowest average score of any group in the district, at 64.

candidates.evidence: Method B's advantage over Method A was greater at rural schools than at urban schools
candidates.explanation: The claim compares two gaps: rural 73 - 64 = 9 versus urban 75 - 72 = 3. Only A states both.

B.rationale: This compares Method B across school types, not Method B's advantage over Method A.

C.rationale: This shows an advantage at both, but not that it was greater at rural schools.

D.rationale: One group's score does not compare the size of the advantage at the two school types.

hints: The claim is about a difference between two differences.

strategy.explanation: Compute each school type's gap first.

candidates.remember: When a claim compares advantages, compare the gaps, not the raw scores.
candidates.revision_note: S014-03 resubmitted unchanged in content and relabelled easy: both blind solvers judged it easy (about 80%).
